metadata.title: Understanding Skill Gaps in Firms: Results of the PIAAC Employer Module

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD Skills Studies report uses the PIAAC Employer Survey Module implemented in five European countries (Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, and the Slovak Republic) with a reference year of 2020. The report describes the Employer Module as a consistent, standardised employer survey component of PIAAC, implemented as part of the European Continuing Vocational Training Survey (CVTS) in 2021–2022. The excerpt provided does not specify whether complex survey weights or replicate weights were applied in the analysis, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or BRR/JRR). For analysts using the underlying PIAAC Employer Module microdata, the appropriate approach would be to apply the survey design weights supplied with the dataset to produce population-representative estimates; however, this report text excerpt does not provide enough methodological detail to confirm the exact weighting and replication scheme used.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Skills Studies report presents results from the PIAAC Employer Survey Module on skill gaps, designed to capture employers’ perspectives on current and future skill needs and the human resource practices used to address them. The Employer Module was implemented in five European countries—Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, and the Slovak Republic—during 2021–2022, as part of the European Continuing Vocational Training Survey (CVTS), with a reference year of 2020. The report positions the Employer Module as complementary to the PIAAC household survey by providing additional evidence on skill mismatches and employer practices, enabling cross-country comparisons. In the provided excerpt, no student-level microdata analytic strategy, PV-based scaling, or ML modeling is described; therefore, no predictive metrics or benchmark effects can be extracted here. The excerpt also does not specify missing-data or weighting/replication procedures, limiting methodological transparency for any downstream quantitative re-use.
